title: Water system monitoring, controls and Part 11 | Aquemi
meta: Online TOC to USP <643>, conductivity to USP <645> stage 1 and audit trails to 21 CFR Part 11 and Annex 11, on PLC and SCADA validated to GAMP 5.
eyebrow: MONITORING AND CONTROLS · USP <643> · USP <645> · 21 CFR PART 11 · GAMP 5
headline: Water quality data you can release on and defend in an inspection
lead: We build the controls and online monitoring for Purified Water (PW) and Water for Injection (WFI) systems so every release decision rests on a record an inspector can trace: total organic carbon (TOC) against the USP <643> limit of 0.50 mg/L on an analyzer with documented system suitability, conductivity against the USP <645> stage 1 table on the raw, non-temperature-compensated reading, and an audit trail that meets 21 CFR Part 11 and EU GMP Annex 11. The software follows the GAMP 5 lifecycle, and the specifications, test records and traceability your validation team needs are written as we build it.

blocks.h: Your water is released on data. The data is what gets inspected.
body: Once online TOC and conductivity are qualified, the numbers they record are the release evidence for every batch that used the water. An inspector reviewing your water system does not stop at the result. They ask for the raw conductivity and temperature behind it, the last TOC system suitability test, who changed an alarm limit and why, which alarms were acknowledged without action, and whether the audit trail has been reviewed.

Data integrity findings in water systems usually come from a small set of gaps: a transmitter that shows only a temperature-compensated value, an operator panel with shared logins, a historian whose clock drifts from the programmable logic controller (PLC), alarm limits changed with no reason recorded, or an audit trail that exists but nobody reviews. The FDA's 2018 questions and answers on data integrity and current good manufacturing practice (CGMP), the PIC/S guidance PI 041-1 and the MHRA's GxP data integrity guidance all address them. Health Canada is a PIC/S member and applies the same expectations.

We design against each of those gaps at the specification stage, test them at factory acceptance testing (FAT), and hand you the evidence, so the controls are something your quality unit can defend rather than something it has to work around.

body: Most conductivity transmitters display a value compensated to 25 °C, because it is easier to trend. USP <645> stage 1 does not use it. The test compares the uncompensated conductivity with the table value for the measured temperature, rounded down to the next 5 °C step. Compensation algorithms are written for ordinary waters, and in ultrapure water at loop temperatures they can move the reading enough to pass water that the compendial test would send to stage 2, or the reverse.

So we record both. The historian stores the raw conductivity and the temperature as the compendial record, and the stage 1 limit is looked up for each reading from the USP table. The compensated value is kept for trending and is labelled as such on every screen and report, so nobody releases on the wrong number.

blocks.caption: Instruments report to a programmable logic controller (PLC) that runs sequences, interlocks, divert and sanitization, and keeps running if every layer above it fails. Operators work at a local human-machine interface (HMI) with individual logins. A supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system and historian stores the quality data, the audit trail and the alarm history, with clocks synchronized to one time source. The historian connects to your plant network, building management system or plant historian through a firewall and demilitarized zone (DMZ) segmented in line with ISA/IEC 62443. Remote support, where you choose it, enters only through a connection you open, control and log.

blocks.h: Risk-based testing, not a stack of screenshots
body: GAMP 5 (second edition, 2022) and the FDA's computer software assurance (CSA) guidance for production and quality system software (finalized in 2025, revised in 2026, written for medical device manufacturers and widely applied in pharma), both ask for testing scaled to risk and for the use of supplier testing where it is well documented. We apply that thinking within your validation policy. Functions that touch product quality, such as divert, quality alarms, sanitization temperature and the audit trail, get scripted tests with recorded evidence. Low-risk display functions can be verified with unscripted or exploratory testing.

Because we write and test the PLC code ourselves and run FAT on the full system, your team can leverage the FAT records in OQ instead of repeating them, if your procedures allow it and the protocols are approved before execution. Your validation team approves the strategy and owns the final computerized system validation.

blocks.h: Questions validation, QA and IT teams ask

items.q: How can our QA team check your controls and validation approach without a prior plant audit record?
items.a: Before you order, review the sample FAT protocol and turnover package, the functional and design specifications for your system and the traceability matrix from each requirement to its test. Your QA team can audit [our software development and change control procedure] and witness the controls FAT.

items.q: Do we get full access to the PLC and HMI code, or are we locked in?
items.a: [Confirm: application code delivered unlocked with the turnover package, and who owns it.] The software version and checksum seen at FAT are recorded, so you can show an inspector that the code running is the code that was tested.

items.q: How do you test the controls at FAT before shipment?
items.a: Every input and output is checked, every sequence, alarm and interlock is run on water, and audit trail entries, user access levels and recovery after a power failure are tested against the functional specification. The FAT and SAT page lists each test case and what IQ/OQ can leverage.

items.q: Can you fit new controls to a skid or loop from another manufacturer?
items.a: Yes, as an upgrade: we survey the instruments and valves you keep, write the functional specification against your current qualified state and plan the cut-over and requalification. See Upgrades and retrofits.

items.q: Can we release water on online TOC and conductivity?
items.a: Yes, for those two attributes, when the instruments are qualified, the sample point represents the water used and your procedures say so. USP <643> and <645> both allow online measurement. Online conductivity covers stage 1 only; a stage 1 failure goes to stages 2 and 3 in the laboratory. Microbial counts and, for WFI, bacterial endotoxin stay laboratory tests unless you qualify an alternative method.

items.q: Our transmitters show temperature-compensated conductivity. Is that a problem?
items.a: For trending, no. For USP <645> stage 1, the compendial record must be the uncompensated conductivity with the measured temperature, compared with the table value for that temperature rounded down to the 5 °C step. We configure transmitters and the historian to store both and label which is which. On an existing system, this is one of the first things we check.

items.q: How often does the online TOC analyzer need system suitability?
items.a: USP <643> requires system suitability, with a response efficiency between 85 % and 115 % on the sucrose and 1,4-benzoquinone standards, but does not fix the interval for online instruments. It is set in your procedures, usually after calibration and at a frequency you justify from the analyzer's history. We perform it at SAT and write the procedure into the maintenance manual.

No system is compliant on its own; your site is, by technical controls in the system plus procedures. We supply the technical controls: audit trail, access control, electronic signatures, record protection and backups. The Part 11 and Annex 11 assessment shows, clause by clause, which controls are in the system and which need a procedure at your site, such as account administration and audit trail review.

Your validation team approves the strategy and owns the computerized system validation. We supply the specifications, the risk assessment, the traceability matrix and executed FAT, SAT and OQ records written so they can be leveraged under your procedures.

items.q: Can you connect to our plant historian, and where does the Part 11 boundary sit?
items.a: Yes, through OPC UA or another standard protocol. We agree in the functional specification which system holds the original record. If your plant historian is the record, ours buffers data through a network loss so nothing is missing; if ours is the record, yours receives a copy for dashboards.

items.q: Our IT team will not allow remote access to GMP equipment.
items.a: Then we do not install it. The system runs and records fully without any outside connection. If you later allow read-only telemetry or supervised sessions, they connect through your DMZ under your IT and change control, with every session logged.

items.q: Who sets the alert and action levels?
items.a: You do, with our input. At handover there is little data, so we start from your specification and the generator's design margin, then recommend alert levels from qualification data, as Annex 1, 6.13 expects, and reassess them once routine monitoring builds history.

items.q: Can you fix data integrity gaps on an existing water system?
items.a: Yes. We start with a gap assessment against Part 11, Annex 11 and USP <645>: shared logins, missing audit trail, compensated-only conductivity, unsynchronized clocks, paper recorders. Then we propose an upgrade scoped to the gaps, with a requalification plan agreed with your quality unit before work starts. See upgrades and requalification.

items.q: Who calibrates the instruments and maintains the software after handover?
items.a: Our service team, from [service locations], with a stated response time of [response time, hours]. A service plan covers calibration, TOC system suitability, UV lamps, ozone sensors, backups and software patches under your change control. Every visit ends with a signed report.
